## CLINICAL RECOMMENDATION

The retrieved evidence base does not directly address the prognosis of root canal-treated cracked teeth stratified by crack extent — no systematic review, RCT, or cohort study in this set specifically evaluates cracked tooth survival or endodontic outcome by crack depth, extension to the pulpal floor, or subgingival propagation. Clinicians should therefore treat any prognostic figures used at chairside as provisional. What this evidence base *does* establish that bears on the case is that (a) single-visit and multiple-visit root canal treatment yield equivalent healing and survival, so visit number should not be the prognostic driver in cracked teeth [[PMID:27905673]], and (b) when a cracked tooth still has vital pulp with reversible pulpitis, vital pulp therapy with calcium silicate cements (MTA/Biodentine) carries success rates of 84–86% at 2–3 years and should be considered before committing to full RCT [[PMID:33222178]] [[PMID:40886932]]. From the wider literature (which this search did not return), cracks confined to the crown with no periodontal probing defect have markedly better post-RCT survival than cracks extending subgingivally or to the pulpal floor, and cuspal-coverage restoration is critical — but this cannot be cited from the papers retrieved.

---

## EVIDENCE SUMMARY

**Cochrane Reviews**

The Manfredi Cochrane review (n=3780, 25 RCTs) compared single- vs multiple-visit root canal treatment across mixed indications and found no difference in tooth extraction, radiographic failure (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.68–1.21), swelling, or sinus tract formation, though single-visit treatment produced more first-week pain and analgesic use (Manfredi et al.) [[PMID:27905673]]. Crucially, this review did not stratify by the presence or extent of coronal cracking, so it cannot be used to derive a crack-specific prognosis — only to affirm that visit protocol is not a major prognostic modifier for endodontic healing generally. The Del Fabbro Cochrane review of surgical vs non-surgical retreatment (20 RCTs) similarly did not analyse cracked teeth as a subgroup (Del Fabbro et al.) [[PMID:27759881]].

**Level I — RCTs and Systematic Reviews**

None of the retrieved systematic reviews or RCTs specifically address cracked tooth prognosis after RCT stratified by crack extent (mesial-marginal-ridge only, extension across the pulpal floor, subgingival propagation, or through-and-through fracture). The vital-pulp-therapy syntheses are relevant only insofar as many cracked teeth present with reversible or early irreversible pulpitis: Cushley et al. reported MTA direct pulp cap success of 86% at 1 year and 84% at 2–3 years, significantly better than calcium hydroxide (OR 2.66 at 1 year) [[PMID:33222178]]; Silva et al. found pulpotomy success of ~92% at 1 year with MTA superior to calcium hydroxide [[PMID:37254176]]; and Hatipoğlu et al.'s Bayesian network meta-regression (19 RCTs, n=1733) ranked Biodentine (SUCRA 83%) and MTA (67%) above calcium hydroxide for DPC in mature permanent teeth [[PMID:40886932]]. Coll et al. (2025) reported 24-month VPT success of 91–97% in teeth with normal pulp/reversible pulpitis and 78% five-year full-pulpotomy success in symptomatic irreversible pulpitis without periapical involvement [[PMID:40533920]]. None of these studies identified cracked teeth as a distinct diagnostic category. Zamparini et al. found no difference between bioceramic and epoxy resin sealers for survival or success [[PMID:38606520]], and Karaoğlan et al. reported ~88% healing at 24 months for single- vs two-visit retreatment of asymptomatic teeth with periapical lesions, again with no crack-specific analysis [[PMID:35488883]].

**Level II–V**

The retrieved evidence base contains no prospective cohort, retrospective cohort, case-control study, or case series in this set that quantifies post-RCT survival or periapical healing of cracked teeth by crack extent. This is a substantive gap: the existing published literature outside this retrieval (Krell & Rivera; Tan et al.; Kang et al.; Sim et al.) reports 2–5-year survival in the 85–90% range for cracked teeth without probing defects and ≤50–60% when cracks extend subgingivally or to the pulpal floor, but those studies are not represented here and cannot be cited.

From the wider literature, which this search did not return: crack prognosis after RCT is strongly determined by (1) whether the crack is confined to the crown vs extending subgingivally or to the pulpal floor, (2) probing depth defects (isolated periodontal pockets >6 mm along the crack signal poor prognosis), and (3) timely full-coverage cuspal-protection restoration. Cracks limited to dentin with no periodontal defect have reported 5-year survival >85%, whereas cracks reaching the pulpal floor or with isolated deep pockets have survival rates commonly reported below 50%. These figures are provided as clinical orientation only and are not supported by the retrieved evidence set.

**Cochrane Reviews**

The Manfredi et al. Cochrane review of single- vs multi-visit RCT (25 RCTs, 3,780 participants) found no difference in tooth extraction, radiological failure, or complication rates between visit protocols, though single-visit patients reported more postoperative pain and analgesic use [[PMID:27905673]]. This review did not stratify outcomes by cracked tooth status or crack extent, so it provides only general procedural context, not crack-specific prognostic data. Del Fabbro et al.'s Cochrane review of surgical vs non-surgical retreatment (20 RCTs) similarly did not address cracked teeth as a subgroup [[PMID:27759881]].

**Level I — RCTs and Systematic Reviews**

None of the Level I systematic reviews or RCTs retrieved (covering vital pulp therapy, pulp capping materials, revitalization, bioceramic sealers, or retreatment protocols) specifically analyzed cracked tooth outcomes by crack extent. Karaoğlan et al.'s RCT of single- vs two-visit retreatment (n=100, 24-month follow-up) identified preoperative lesion size and initial root filling length as significant prognostic factors — variables that often correlate with crack severity in cracked teeth — but did not enroll or analyze cracked teeth specifically [[PMID:35488883]]. Matoug-Elwerfelli et al.'s systematic review of VPT in traumatised teeth addressed complicated crown/crown-root fractures rather than cracks and reported partial pulpotomy success of 82.9–100%, but this addresses fracture management rather than post-RCT prognosis of cracked teeth [[PMID:35348216]].

**Level II — Prospective Studies / Level IIIa — Retrospective Cohort Studies / Level IIIb — Case-Control Studies / Level IV — Case Series / Level V — Expert Opinion**

No studies retrieved in this evidence set specifically address cracked tooth prognosis after RCT stratified by crack extent (crown-only, crown-to-root, subgingival extension, pulpal floor involvement, or split tooth). This is a substantial gap in the retrieved evidence, and any recommendation on this topic must acknowledge that gap rather than extrapolate from unrelated endodontic outcome data.

**Recommendation for next steps in evidence gathering:** A targeted search using terms such as "cracked tooth" AND ("survival" OR "prognosis" OR "outcome") AND ("root canal" OR "endodontic"), and specifically the Krell & Rivera, Tan et al., Kang et al., and AAE cracked tooth classification literature, is required to answer this question with grounded evidence.
